text: The National Liberal Party (German: Nationalliberale Partei, NLP) was a liberal political party of the North German Confederation and the German Empire that flourished between 1867 and 1918. During the Prussian-led unification of Germany, it became the dominant party in the Reichstag, supporting both liberal and nationalist ideals, though it contained two ideological wings reflecting its Hegelian and idealistic roots: one emphasizing state power through the Nationalstaat and the other advocating civil liberties through the Rechtsstaat. Despite this internal division, the party remained pivotal in the decades after unification by cooperating with both the Progressives and the Free Conservatives. A first national liberal parliamentary group formed in the Prussian House of Representatives in response to a constitutional conflict triggered by Minister President Otto von Bismarck in 1862, when he used the Lückentheorie ("Gap Theory") and his "Blood and Iron" speech to override liberal opposition and proceed with military reforms. After Bismarck's victory over Austria in the Seven Weeks' War of 1866, particularly at the Battle of Königgrätz on 3 July, many liberals set aside their differences due to support for Bismarck's foreign policy. On 3 September, the liberal division was confirmed when 19 National Liberal deputies voted for Bismarck's Indemnity Law, which formalized his circumvention of parliamentary budgetary rights. Supporters believed opposition was futile because Bismarck had the backing of King Wilhelm I, and accepting the law would improve their position to push for greater freedoms. This first National Liberal faction was established on 17 November around Eduard Lasker and Hans Victor von Unruh. The party was founded during the North German federal election on 12 February 1867, gathering support from Prussian annexed territories like Hanover and Hesse-Nassau and other Confederation states, emerging as the largest faction in the North German Reichstag. An inaugural declaration was adopted on 12 June, and Rudolf von Bennigsen became the first party chairman. The party championed the interests of the Grand Burgher dynasties, business magnates, and nationalist-minded Protestant circles of the educated bourgeoisie (Bildungsbürgertum), with its manifesto focusing on national unification and Bismarck's policies that established a constitutional monarchy and a highly industrialized German nation state. From 1871 to 1879, the National Liberals were Bismarck's chief allies in the Reichstag, strongly supporting the anti-Catholic Kulturkampf measures and the Anti-Socialist Laws. In the first all-German federal election on 3 March 1871, the party received 30.1% of the votes, securing 119 seats and becoming the largest group in the Reichstag, with Rudolf von Bennigsen remaining chairman. The party's support enabled the stabilization of the new German state, guiding Bismarck's domestic policies, including the standardization of weights and measurements, the creation of a common German market and the Reichsbank, and the replacement of regional currencies with the Goldmark. Although these liberal economic policies were initially unpopular during the 1870s recession, they laid the foundation for Germany's economic boom at the turn of the 19th century. In 1879, Bismarck's alliance with the National Liberals ended when he abandoned free trade and introduced a tariff, a shift driven by economic pressures following the Panic of 1873. This protectionist policy violated liberal principles and marked Bismarck's "conservative turn," altering the political climate and straining relations with leading German liberals. The National Liberals lost their dominant status in 1880 when the left-wing split off and merged with the Progress Party to form the German Free-minded Party by 1884. The remaining members aligned with the Conservatives, becoming key supporters of Alfred von Tirpitz's Fleet Acts starting in 1898, which triggered a naval arms race with Britain until World War I. In the 1887 federal election, a right-wing cartel of National Liberals, Conservatives, and Free Conservatives secured a parliamentary majority for Bismarck until his resignation in 1890. Regarding the Kulturkampf, Bismarck distanced himself from the liberals, reconciled with a less confrontational Pope, and began political cooperation with the Catholic Centre Party. Historian Hajo Holborn notes the contradictions between the Kulturkampf and liberal values, with David Blackbourn stating that the liberal attacks on the Catholic Church left a political legacy contrary to liberal intentions—making liberals dependent on Bismarck and helping to consolidate political Catholicism in Germany. In 1905, Ernst Bassermann became chairman, succeeding Johannes von Miquel. The party became closely linked with big business, maintaining strong ties to industrialist advocacy groups and imperialist and nationalist organizations like the Pan-German League. Increasingly threatened by the rise of the Social Democrats, the party grew more conservative, though it remained divided between a liberal wing seeking to strengthen ties with dissident left-liberals and a right-wing faction supporting protectionist policies and closer relations with the Conservatives and the imperial government. During World War I, most National Liberals, including left-wing leader Gustav Stresemann, supported the imperial government's expansionist goals while also calling for domestic reform. After the war, the party dissolved: Stresemann led the main body, including moderate and conservative elements, into the conservative liberal German People's Party; the left wing merged with the Progressive People's Party to form the German Democratic Party; and the far-right wing joined the German National People's Party.
